headline: Pennsylvania: Shapiro's nearly $70 million campaign swamps Garrity's late skill-games cash
dek: Gov. Josh Shapiro raised about six times what Stacy Garrity did and had the airwaves to himself for months. Skill-games money paid for her ads in the last weeks. Shapiro won by 22 points.
summary: Shapiro outraised Garrity about six to one, dominated TV for months and won by 22 points; skill-games donors funded her late ads.

paras.text: Pennsylvania's governor's race pitted a campaign with plenty of money against one with very little, until the final three weeks. Gov. Josh Shapiro, the Democratic incumbent, beat Stacy Garrity, the Republican state treasurer, 3,012,429 votes to 1,908,797, according to Associated Press results published by The New York Times. That is a 22.1-point margin in a state that voted Republican by 1.7 points for president in 2024, a swing of 23.8 points.

The Watch's Federal Election Commission data showed no outside spending in Pennsylvania's federal races, and that data had not yet been fully read. So this report follows the governor's race. Candidates in that race report to the Pennsylvania Department of State, and the figures below come from those filings as reported by the state's press.

The gap was there from the start. Since 2025, Shapiro has reported more than $63.7 million in total contributions, compared to Garrity, who has reported $10.6 million, according to City & State Pennsylvania's reading of the state records. Pittsburgh's PublicSource found that Shapiro collected about half of his campaign cash from out of state, compared to 7% for Garrity.

The Democratic Governors Association, a party-aligned committee that works to elect Democratic governors, was Shapiro's biggest single source over the summer. It gave $1.25 million to his campaign. Unions gave Shapiro about $2 million combined; the largest single donation from that sector was $500,000 from public workers union AFSCME. In the fall, his largest donations included $500,000 each from Thomas Hagen, former CEO of Erie Insurance Group, and Margaret Hardy, former owner and CEO of 84 Lumber.

For most of the year, Garrity relied on Pennsylvania donors. She continued to count former GOP state party Chair Bob Asher among her biggest supporters. The big Republican spenders stayed out of the race: no top GOP groups, such as the Republican Governors Association or the Jeffrey Yass-backed Commonwealth Leaders Fund, have purchased TV ads supporting Garrity, The Inquirer reported in September. Yass's network spent in other races instead. Spotlight PA reported that Students First, a PAC funded by Yass, has spent $23.5 million this year, much of it on legislative contests.

Garrity's money changed after the Oct. 7 debate. There she backed legalizing skill games, the slot-like machines found in bars and clubs, with a tax of $500 per machine per month. Between Sept. 15 and Oct. 19, according to WHP-TV, 84% of the $5.3 million came from three donors who have interests in skill games. The Pennsylvania Amusement and Music Machine Association, a trade group representing skill-game operators and other coin-operated entertainment businesses, contributed $2 million. Another $2 million came from John D. Conley, the Pittsburgh-based owner of skill games developer Pinnacle Vending. Spotlight PA reported that Conley had been accused of running an "illegal gambling enterprise" with his father. The trade group then contributed $600,000 to Garrity's campaign on Oct. 20, and another $250,000 the next day. Garrity has said the money does not impact her stance on skill games. The counts of the industry's total vary with the date of the report. By Election Day, The Inquirer put it at more than $6 million from skill games industry backers.

Shapiro's money went to television. In early October The Inquirer counted the $30 million Shapiro has already spent on TV and digital ads in the race so far. His main attack ad used clips of Garrity's own words. It quotes Garrity saying in a series of clips that "48 of 76 of out counties in Pennsylvania are rural, so there are a lot of areas where you can put data centers", and labels her the state's top fan of data centers. According to AdImpact, that ad has been viewed 416 million times. In another, Shapiro boasts about his efforts to cap energy costs.

Garrity attacked first on the same issue. Her ad said Shapiro had "sold us out" to Amazon's data-center projects and claimed "Shapiro pocketed over $5 million in political contributions from out-of-state data center developers." A reporting review found that a bulk of the donations the Garrity campaign cited don't come from data center developers at all. AdImpact counted about 802,000 views of her ad in the Philadelphia market. In one late-September week, Shapiro spent more than $2.4 million on ads. His GOP opponent, Stacy Garrity, spent $672. Before that, most of her ad money had gone to a digital social media video campaign called "Twilight Justice".

The skill-games money paid for her closing ads. Between Sept. 15 and Oct. 19, Garrity spent $3.3 million, mostly on TV advertising and direct mail. The best-known of these ads showed an AI-generated Shapiro. WESA reported that it ran with no watermark or text on the screen and that the fake Shapiro did not say he was AI until about 45 seconds in. Pennsylvania has no law requiring that disclosure. Shapiro's spokesman, Manuel Bonder, called the ad "cheap" and "dishonest." Garrity told KDKA-TV that she stands by the ad.
Did the money buy the seat?

The side that spent more won, by a wide margin. Shapiro's campaign has vastly outspent Garrity's, dropping almost $70 million since the start of 2025 compared to roughly $7 million in the same time period. Not all of Shapiro's money went to his own race. He gave $5.6 million to the Pennsylvania Democratic Party to aid their statewide effort to flip seats in both the state and federal legislatures.

The money is not the only explanation. Shapiro was a popular incumbent, and the Siena poll for The Inquirer and The New York Times had him holding a 21-point lead in September, before Garrity's late ads ran. He won by 22. The Inquirer concluded that the late skill-games push gave Garrity some momentum on the air but it was not enough to change Tuesday's result. The Times Leader reported that Republicans spent much of their money defending the Legislature, leaving not much room for Garrity to garner their aid. Spending reports covering the last weeks of the race are still to come. Until they arrive, the totals here are incomplete.
